items.title: Two regressions, one correlation
items.prose: A study fits two regressions on the same ten pairs of returns. Regressing $y$ on $x$ gives a slope of 0.75. Regressing $x$ on $y$ gives a slope of 0.27.
items.question: What is the correlation of $x$ and $y$?

feedback.correct: The slopes multiply to $r^2 = 0.2025$, so $r = 0.45$.
feedback.generic: Multiply the two slopes, then take the square root.

byKey.r-squared: You stopped at the product of the slopes. That is $r^2$. Take its square root.
byKey.mean-slopes: You averaged the slopes. The correlation is their geometric mean, not the arithmetic one.
byKey.one-slope: You gave one slope. A slope equals $r$ only when both spreads are equal.

explain.text: The two slopes multiply to $r^2$: $0.75 \times 0.27 = 0.2025$. The square root, with the sign of the slopes, gives $r = 0.45$.

items.title: Which pattern
items.prose: A venue publishes 5,000 trading halts. Each is a start minute and an end minute, and the halt does not include its end minute.
items.question: You must report the most halts in force at one minute. Which approach fits?

options.text: Sort the starts and ends together, then sweep with a counter
Build a trie from the minute numbers written as strings
options.why: A trie answers prefix questions about strings. Overlapping halts have no prefix structure.

options.text: XOR every start minute with every end minute together
options.why: XOR finds a value left unpaired. Counting overlaps needs a running total.

options.text: Keep a monotonic deque of start minutes over a fixed window
options.why: A fixed window needs one width. These halts all have different lengths.

feedback.correct: Turn each halt into a $+1$ and a $-1$ event, sort them and sweep.
feedback.generic: Ask what changes over time: how many halts are in force.

explain.text: Turn each halt into two events: $+1$ at its start and $-1$ at its end. Sort the events and add them up in order. The largest running total is the answer, and the sort costs $O(n \log n)$.

items.title: A seek against a round trip
items.prose: A disk seek takes 10 ms. A round trip inside one data centre takes 500 µs.
items.question: How many data-centre round trips fit in the time of one disk seek?

feedback.generic: Write both times in the same unit, then divide the larger by the smaller.

byKey.inverted: You divided the round trip by the seek. Divide the longer time by the shorter one.
byKey.tenth-of-ms: You read 500 µs as 0.05 ms. It is 0.5 ms, so the quotient is 20.
byKey.units-ignored: You divided 10 by 5 and dropped the units. Convert 10 ms to 10,000 µs first.

explain.text: 10 ms is 10,000 µs. Divide by 500 µs to get 20 round trips.

items.title: The best of six signals
items.prose: You test six candidate signals on the same history. The best has $p = 0.012$. You want the chance of any false positive across all six to stay at 5%.
items.question: What do you say about the best signal?

options.text: No. It must beat $0.05/6 \approx 0.0083$, and it does not.
Yes. 0.012 is below 0.05, so it passes the test.
options.why: You compared with 0.05 as if you had tried one signal. Six looks need a stricter bar.

options.text: No. There is only a 1.2% chance that the signal is real.
options.why: You read $p$ as the chance the signal is real. It is the chance of a result this extreme if there is no effect.

options.text: It cannot be judged until you see the other five $p$-values.
options.why: The Bonferroni bar depends only on how many tests you ran, not on the other results.

feedback.correct: Each of six tests must clear $0.05/6 \approx 0.0083$. The $p$ of 0.012 does not.
feedback.generic: Divide the 5% by the number of signals you tried.

explain.text: With six looks, each test must beat $0.05/6 \approx 0.0083$ to keep the chance of any false positive at 5%. The best $p$ of 0.012 does not. The same test in another form: the corrected $p$ is $6 \times 0.012 = 0.072$, above 0.05.

items.title: Read the rules, then trace
items.prose: An assessment describes a margin account that starts at £500. Each day, in this order: (1) if the balance is below £400, add £250. (2) Add the day's profit or loss. (3) If the balance is above £700, withdraw half of the amount above £700. The six daily results are $-120$, $-90$, $+60$, $+400$, $-250$ and $-180$, in £.
items.question: What is the balance after day 6?

feedback.correct: The balances run 380, 540, 600, 850, 600 and 420.
feedback.generic: Apply the three rules in order each day and write the balance down after day 1.

byKey.withdraw-all: You withdrew all the amount above £700. The rule takes half of it.
byKey.never-withdraw: You skipped rule 3. Day 4 ends above £700, so half of the excess leaves.
byKey.half-balance: You withdrew half of the whole balance. Only half of the amount above £700 leaves.

explain.text: Day 1 ends at £380. Day 2 tops up to £630 and ends at £540, and day 3 at £600. Day 4 reaches £1,000, so £150 leaves, giving £850, then £600 and £420.

items.title: The cost of wrong guesses
items.prose: A loop tests 2,000,000 prices with `if (p < limit)`. The test is true for 30% of them, in no pattern. The predictor always guesses the likelier outcome. Each wrong guess costs 14 cycles.
items.question: How many cycles do the wrong guesses cost in all?

feedback.correct: The wrong guesses are 30% of 2,000,000, so 600,000 of them. At 14 cycles that is 8.4 million.
feedback.generic: Count the wrong guesses first, then multiply by the cost of one.

byKey.coin-flip: You assumed half are wrong. The predictor picks the likelier side, so only 30% are.
byKey.every-pass: You charged every pass 14 cycles. Only the wrong guesses pay.
byKey.likelier-side: You counted the 70% that are false. The predictor guesses those, so the 30% are the misses.

explain.text: The predictor always guesses the likelier outcome, so it is wrong on the 30% that go the other way. That is $2{,}000{,}000 \times 0.3 = 600{,}000$ wrong guesses. At 14 cycles each, the cost is 8.4 million cycles.

items.title: How high can the third correlation go
items.prose: Three assets, A, B and C. The correlation of A with B is 0.8. The correlation of B with C is $-0.5$.
items.question: What is the largest correlation that A and C can have? Give it to 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The range is $-0.4 \pm 0.5196$, so the top is 0.1196.
feedback.generic: Use the product of the two correlations, then add the half-width from the determinant.

byKey.product: You gave the centre of the range, $0.8 \times (-0.5)$. Add the half-width to reach the top.
byKey.half-width: You gave the half-width alone. Add it to the centre, $-0.4$.
byKey.floor: You subtracted the half-width. That is the lowest value, not the highest.

explain.text: The correlation matrix must be positive semidefinite, so its determinant is at least zero. That gives $\rho_{AC} = \rho_{AB}\rho_{BC} \pm \sqrt{(1-\rho_{AB}^2)(1-\rho_{BC}^2)}$. Here it is $-0.4 \pm 0.5196$, so the top is 0.1196.

items.title: Count the pops from the back
items.prose: A monotonic deque of indices finds the maximum of every window of 4 prices. Before each push it pops from the back every price at most the new one. It pops from the front when that index leaves the window. The prices, in order, are 7, 3, 9, 4, 6, 8, 2, 5, 5, 1.
items.question: How many pops from the back happen in all?

feedback.correct: The back pops are 2, 1, 1, 1 and 1, which total 6.
feedback.generic: Walk the prices one at a time and count only the pops from the back.

byKey.fronts: You counted pops from the front, 2. The question asks about the back.
byKey.both: You added the 2 front pops. Count back pops only.
byKey.strict: You popped only smaller prices. The rule says at most the new one, so the second 5 pops the first.

explain.text: The 9 pops 3 and 7: 2 pops. The 6, 8 and first 5 pop 4, 6 and 2, and the second 5 pops the first. In all, $2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6$ pops from the back.

items.title: Count the misses of a stride
items.prose: An array of `double` (8 bytes each) starts on a 64-byte line boundary. A loop reads `a[0]`, `a[3]`, `a[6]` and so on, 1,000 reads in all. The cache starts cold and is big enough to keep every line it loads.
items.question: How many of the reads miss the cache?

feedback.correct: The reads span lines 0 to 374, and every line in between is touched once: 375 misses.
feedback.generic: Find the line of the last read, then ask whether any line is skipped.

byKey.every-read: You counted every read as a miss. Reads 24 bytes apart often land in the same 64-byte line.
byKey.unit-stride: You counted for 1,000 neighbouring doubles, 8,000 bytes. These reads span about 24,000 bytes.
byKey.one-in-three: You divided by 3. A line holds about 2.7 reads here, so count the lines covered instead.

explain.text: Read $k$ is at byte $24k$, so the last is at byte 23,976, in line 374. The stride is below 64 bytes, so every line from 0 to 374 is touched. That makes 375 misses.

items.title: A determinant without expanding
items.prose: Let $w = (1, 2, 2, 4)^\top$ and $A = 2I + 3ww^\top$, a 4 by 4 matrix.
items.question: What is $\det A$?

feedback.correct: The eigenvalues are 77, 2, 2 and 2, and their product is 616.
feedback.generic: Find the eigenvalue along $w$, then count the others.

byKey.no-identity: You gave $8 \times 75$. The eigenvalue along $w$ is $2 + 75 = 77$, since the $2I$ adds to it.
byKey.all-fours: You used $2^4 \times 77$. Only three eigenvalues equal 2. The fourth is 77.
byKey.one-eigenvalue: You gave the largest eigenvalue. The determinant is the product of all four.

explain.text: The matrix $ww^\top$ has rank one, with eigenvalue $w^\top w = 25$ along $w$ and 0 on the other three directions. So $A$ has eigenvalues $2 + 3 \times 25 = 77$ and $2, 2, 2$. The determinant is $77 \times 2^3 = 616$.

items.title: Evaluate with signs
items.prose: A parser handles `+ - * /`. The operators `*` and `/` bind tighter, and equal ranks go left to right. A minus sign directly before a number belongs to that number. Division truncates toward zero.
items.question: What is `25 + 7 * -4 / 3 + 17 / -5`?

feedback.generic: Do the products and quotients first, truncating each toward zero.

byKey.floor: You rounded down. Truncation toward zero gives $-9$ and $-3$, not $-10$ and $-4$.
byKey.no-signs: You dropped the two minus signs. They flip the sign of each term.
byKey.left-to-right: You ignored precedence. Multiplication and division go before addition.

explain.text: First $7 \times (-4) = -28$, and $-28 / 3$ truncates to $-9$. Next $17 / (-5)$ truncates to $-3$. So the value is $25 - 9 - 3 = 13$.

items.title: Where is the padding
items.prose: `struct Tick { uint8_t side; uint32_t qty; uint16_t venue; uint64_t id; };` Each field starts at a multiple of its own size. The struct's size is a multiple of its largest field. The grid shows its 24 bytes by offset, 8 to a row.

state.caption: 24 bytes, numbered by offset. Each row is 8 bytes.

items.question: Tap every byte that is padding.

feedback.correct: 9 of the 24 bytes are padding: bytes 1 to 3, and bytes 10 to 15.
feedback.generic: Find where each field must start, and mark the bytes skipped before it.

byKey.first-gap-only: You found the gap before `qty` only. `id` must start at 16, so bytes 10 to 15 are skipped too.
byKey.second-gap-only: You found the gap before `id` only. `qty` must start at 4, so bytes 1 to 3 are skipped too.

explain.text: `qty` must start at a multiple of 4, so bytes 1 to 3 are skipped. `id` must start at a multiple of 8, so bytes 10 to 15 are skipped. That is 9 padding bytes in 24.

items.title: Raise the penalty without limit
items.prose: A spread averages 40 ticks. You standardise four features. You fit a ridge and a lasso, each with a constant that the penalty leaves alone. Then you raise $\lambda$ without limit.
items.question: What do the two models forecast in the end?

options.text: 40 for every row. The lasso gets there at a finite $\lambda$. Ridge only approaches it.
0 for every row, because a huge penalty sends every coefficient to zero.
options.why: You penalised the constant too. Here it is left alone, so it keeps the target's average of 40.

options.text: 40 from ridge but 0 from the lasso, since only the lasso has exact zeros.
options.why: Exact zeros apply to the slopes. The constant stays at 40 in both models.

options.text: 40 from the lasso, but ridge never gets near it, because its slopes stay non-zero.
options.why: Ridge slopes stay non-zero but shrink towards zero, so its forecast tends to 40 without reaching it.

feedback.correct: With the slopes gone, only the constant is left, and it equals the average of 40.
feedback.generic: Ask what each penalty does to the slopes, and what is left when they vanish.

explain.text: The constant is outside the penalty, so it settles at the target's mean, 40. The lasso sets every slope to exactly zero once $\lambda$ passes a finite limit. Ridge slopes only shrink towards zero, so its forecast tends to 40 without reaching it.

items.title: A buy order crosses the book
items.prose: Four sell orders rest on the book, as shown. Matching uses price-time priority, and each trade is at the resting order's price. A buy order for 20 units at a limit of 100.5 now arrives.
items.question: Which fills happen, in order?

options.text: D 6 at 100.0, then B 5 and C 8 at 100.5. One unit rests as a bid.
A 10 at 101.0, then B 5 and C 5 at 100.5. Nothing rests.
options.why: You matched in arrival order. Price priority comes first, and A is above the limit anyway.

options.text: D 6, then B 5 and C 8, all at 100.5. One unit rests as a bid.
options.why: You traded at the incoming limit. Each fill happens at the resting order's price, so D trades at 100.0.

options.text: D 6 at 100.0, then C 8 and B 5 at 100.5. One unit rests as a bid.
options.why: You swapped the two orders at 100.5. B arrived before C, so B fills first.

feedback.correct: Best price first: D. Then B before C by arrival. A is above the limit, so one unit rests.
feedback.generic: Sort the sellers by price, then by arrival, and stop at the limit.

explain.text: The lowest price trades first, so D fills 6 at 100.0. The two orders at 100.5 trade in arrival order, B then C, for 13 units in all. A is above the 100.5 limit, so the last unit rests as a bid.

items.title: Why the first loop is slow
items.prose: A program calls `malloc` for a 192 MiB buffer. A loop then writes one byte into each 4 KiB page. That first loop is slow. A second identical loop over the same buffer is far faster.
items.question: What explains the slow first loop?

options.text: Each first write to a page traps into the kernel, which maps a zeroed page.
Each write misses every cache level and waits for the disk.
options.why: New memory is not read from disk. The kernel creates a zeroed page, so there is nothing to fetch.

options.text: A cold TLB makes every write cost as much as a page fault.
options.why: A TLB miss is a hardware page-table walk of tens of cycles. A fault enters the kernel and costs far more.

options.text: `malloc` zeroed the whole buffer when it was called, and the loop pays for it.
options.why: For a large request `malloc` touches no pages. The kernel supplies each page on its first write.

feedback.correct: The buffer is address space until first use. Each first write to a page faults once.
feedback.generic: Ask what the kernel has to do the first time a program touches a page.

explain.text: The 192 MiB is only address space until it is used. The first write to each of its 49,152 pages traps into the kernel, which maps a zeroed page. The second loop finds every page already mapped.

items.title: Share of the first component
items.prose: Two assets have the covariance matrix $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 7 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$, in squared per cent.
items.question: What share of the total variance does the first principal component carry? Give one decimal place.

feedback.correct: The eigenvalues are 8 and 3, so the first carries $8/11 = 72.7\%$.
feedback.generic: Find the eigenvalues from the trace and the determinant, then divide the larger by the trace.

byKey.larger-asset: You gave the larger asset's share of variance, $7/11$. The component mixes both assets and carries more.
byKey.second-component: You gave the second component's share, $3/11$. The first carries the rest.
byKey.half: You assumed two components split the variance evenly. The eigenvalues are 8 and 3.

explain.text: The trace is 11 and the determinant is $7 \times 4 - 2^2 = 24$, so $\lambda^2 - 11\lambda + 24 = 0$ and $\lambda = 8$ or 3. The first component carries $8/11 = 72.7\%$ of the variance.

items.title: Who gets evicted
items.prose: A least recently used cache holds 4 keys. A `get` or a `put` of a stored key counts as a use. A `get` of a missing key changes nothing. A `put` of a new key evicts the least recently used key when the cache is full. The steps are: (1) put P, (2) put Q, (3) put R, (4) put S. Then (5) get Q, (6) put P, (7) put T, (8) get R, (9) put U, (10) get P.
items.question: Fill in the table. Type a single letter in each cell.

rows: Least recently used key after step 10
Most recently used key after step 10

feedback.correct: Step 7 evicts R and step 9 evicts S. After step 10 the order runs Q, T, U, P.
feedback.generic: Write the keys from least to most recently used after every step.

byKey.r0c1: Step 7 evicts the key unused longest. A `get` or `put` of a stored key at steps 5 and 6 moves it to the newest end.
byKey.r1c1: After step 7 the order is S, Q, P, T. The missing `get` of R changes nothing, so the oldest key, S, goes.
byKey.r2c1: Write the keys from oldest to newest use after step 10. The `get` of P at step 10 moves P to the end.
byKey.r3c1: The newest key is the one used last. Step 10 was a `get` of P.

explain.text: Steps 5 and 6 turn P, Q, R, S into R, S, Q, P, so T evicts R. The missed get of R changes nothing, so U evicts S. The final order is Q, T, U, P.

items.title: Two threads, one integer
items.prose: Two threads start together on a shared `int n = 0;` with no lock. Thread A runs `n = n + 2;`. Thread B runs `n = n * 3;`. Each statement reads `n`, calculates, then writes `n`.
items.question: Select all that apply. Which claims hold?

options.text: Some interleavings give a final value of 0.
Making `n` a `std::atomic<int>` removes the data race but not the 0.
With a mutex around each whole statement, the final value is 2 or 6.
The only possible final values are 2 and 6.
options.why: You counted the two whole-statement orders. A write can use a stale read, which gives 0.

options.text: A final value of 8 is possible.
options.why: 8 needs A to read a 6. A reads before it writes, and 6 exists only after A has written.

options.text: Declaring `n` as `volatile int` makes each statement indivisible.
options.why: `volatile` stops the compiler caching `n`. It does not make the read and the write one step.

feedback.correct: Claims a, b and c hold. The final value can be 0, 2 or 6, and never 8.
feedback.generic: Step the two threads through the reads and writes in different orders.

explain.text: If B reads 0, A writes 2 and then B writes 0, the final value is 0. Other orders give 2 and 6, so 0, 2 and 6 are all possible, and 8 is not. An atomic removes the undefined behaviour, but only a mutex per statement forces 2 or 6.

items.title: Beat the index next week
items.prose: An interviewer asks: "Will a given stock beat the index next week?" You answer with a case plan.
items.question: Put the steps in order. Leave out the two that do not belong.

lines.text: Define the label first: the stock's return beats the index's over the next five days
Build features known at each Friday's close, then split by date with a gap of five days
On the training weeks, find the baseline hit rate by always guessing the more common label
On the training weeks, fit a simple model
Compare the two hit rates on the test weeks
Report the gap with an interval and the weeks where it fails
Shuffle the weeks so train and test look alike
lines.why: Shuffling puts later weeks in training, so the test score is better than the future will be.

lines.text: Tune the model on the test weeks until it beats the baseline
lines.why: Tuning on the test weeks uses them up. The reported hit rate is then too high.

feedback.correct: Define the label, build features and split with a gap, then find the baseline and fit in either order. Compare and report.
feedback.generic: A label that looks five days ahead overlaps its neighbours, so the split needs a gap.

explain.text: The label looks five days ahead, so train and test weeks overlap unless a gap separates them. The baseline and the model both use the training weeks, so either can come first. Compare them on the test weeks, then report the gap with its uncertainty.

items.title: The next higher price
items.prose: Daily closing prices sit in a list. For each day we want the next later day with a higher close, in one pass over the list.
items.question: Put the steps in order. Leave out the two that do not belong.

lines.text: Start with an empty stack of days still waiting for a higher close
For each day, pop every waiting day with a lower close and record this day as its answer
Push the new day onto the stack
After the last day, mark the days still on the stack as having no higher close
Compare each day with every later day and stop at the first higher close
lines.why: That gives the right answers but takes quadratic time. The stack touches each day once.

lines.text: Push the new day first, then pop the days with a lower close
lines.why: The new day would sit on top and block the pops, so the lower days never leave.

feedback.correct: Start empty, pop and record, push, then mark what is left.
feedback.generic: Ask when a day leaves the stack, and which days are still on it at the end.

explain.text: A day waits on the stack until a higher close arrives. Each day is pushed once and popped at most once, so the pass is linear. Days still waiting at the end have no higher close.

items.title: Spend the minutes
items.prose: An online assessment gives 70 minutes and four problems. Each can be solved in full, solved in part, or skipped. You earn the marks only if you spend the minutes shown.
items.question: What is the most marks you can earn in 70 minutes?

feedback.correct: Part of P1, all of P2, parts of P3 and P4: 82 marks in 66 minutes.
feedback.generic: Compare every mix of skip, part and full that fits inside 70 minutes.

byKey.full-only: You allowed only full solutions, which reach 75. Partial credit lifts the total.
byKey.fill-the-clock: You found a plan worth 80 that uses all 70 minutes. A plan using 66 minutes is worth 82.
byKey.all-partial: You took every part and left 27 minutes unused. Spend them on a full solution.

explain.text: Take part of P1, all of P2, and parts of P3 and P4: $12 + 40 + 10 + 20 = 82$ marks in $9 + 36 + 6 + 15 = 66$ minutes. All 81 mixes were checked. Full solutions alone reach only 75.

items.title: Claims about a weak signal
items.prose: A researcher tests a daily signal on a liquid futures contract. Its correlation with the next day's return is 0.04 over 2,500 days.
items.question: Select all that apply. Which of these statements hold?

options.text: The $t$-statistic is about 2, so the evidence is borderline.
A correlation of 0.02 would need about 10,000 days to reach the same $t$-statistic.
A gross edge of 4 basis points is lost to costs of 5 basis points a round trip.
Doubling the sample halves the standard error of the correlation.
options.why: You halved it. The standard error falls with $\sqrt{n}$, so doubling the data cuts it by $\sqrt{2}$ only.

options.text: A 21-day centred moving average of price is a safe feature, since it is smooth.
options.why: A centred window holds 10 future days. The feature uses information that does not exist at the forecast time.

options.text: A signal that held from 2010 to 2015 will hold in the next five years, since markets are stable.
options.why: You assumed the regime stays put. Relationships drift, so test on later data and expect some decay.

feedback.correct: Statements a, b and c hold. The other three miss the square root, a leak and a regime change.
feedback.generic: Check each statement with a number, a timestamp or a later period.

explain.text: The $t$-statistic is about $r\sqrt{n} = 0.04 \times 50 = 2$, and halving $r$ needs four times the days, so 0.02 needs 10,000. Costs larger than the gross edge leave a loss. A centred window leaks the future, and a regime can change.

items.title: Inputs that expose the bug
items.question: Select all that apply. Which calls return a wrong answer?

options.text: `peak_window_total([6], 1)`
`peak_window_total([2, 3, 5], 3)`
`peak_window_total([4, 1], 2)`
`peak_window_total([], 2)`
options.why: The list is shorter than $k$, so `None` is right, and the code returns it.

options.text: `peak_window_total([1, 2], 3)`
options.why: Two values cannot fill a window of 3. `None` is right, and the code returns it.

options.text: `peak_window_total([5, 1, 4, 2], 2)`
options.why: The list is longer than $k$, so the loop runs and returns 6, which is right.

feedback.correct: The three calls with exactly $k$ values fail: the guard returns `None` for them.
feedback.generic: Find the inputs where the guard `len(xs) <= k` gives the wrong branch.

explain.text: The guard uses `<=`, so a list with exactly $k$ values counts as too short. For those lists the answer is the sum of the whole list. The three calls with exactly $k$ values expose it.

items.title: One feed, thirty servers
items.prose: An exchange sends 2,000 price updates a second. Thirty strategy servers in one rack must each see every update. A server must never act on a gap it has not noticed.
items.question: Which design suits the feed?

options.text: Multicast UDP with a sequence number on each message, and a TCP channel to ask for a replay
One TCP connection from the exchange to each server, so the network guarantees every message
options.why: The exchange sends thirty copies, and one lost packet holds back that server's stream until the retransmit.

options.text: Multicast UDP with no sequence numbers, because the next update replaces a lost one
options.why: A lost message may be a trade or a cancel. Without sequence numbers a server cannot tell it missed one.

options.text: UDP unicast to each server, resent every 10 ms until it is acknowledged
options.why: Acknowledged resends rebuild the delays of TCP, and the exchange still sends thirty copies.

feedback.correct: Multicast sends one copy to all thirty. Sequence numbers expose a gap and a replay repairs it.
feedback.generic: Ask which design sends one copy and still lets a server notice a missing message.

explain.text: Multicast sends one copy that all thirty servers receive. A sequence number on each message shows a server where it missed one. A TCP channel then fetches the missing messages without delaying the live stream.

items.title: Three forecasts of a mean-reverting spread
items.prose: A spread has mean 0, variance 4 and a day-to-day autocorrelation of 0.6. We compare three forecasts of tomorrow's value: today's value, the mean 0, and the fitted $0.6 \times$ today's value.
items.question: By what percentage does the fitted forecast cut the mean squared error of the persistence forecast?

feedback.correct: Persistence has error 3.2 and the fit 2.56. The cut is $1 - 2.56/3.2 = 20\%$.
feedback.generic: Find each mean squared error, then compare the fit with persistence, not with the mean.

byKey.ratio: You gave the ratio of the errors, 80%. The cut is what is left over, $1 - 0.8$.
byKey.against-mean: You compared the fit with the mean forecast, whose error is 4. The question asks about persistence.
byKey.one-minus-phi: You gave $1 - 0.6$. The errors are $2 \times 4 \times 0.4$ and $4 \times 0.64$, and their ratio sets the cut.

explain.text: Persistence errs by $x_{t+1} - x_t$, with variance $2 \times 4 \times (1 - 0.6) = 3.2$. The fitted forecast errs with variance $4 \times (1 - 0.6^2) = 2.56$. The cut is $1 - 2.56/3.2 = 20\%$.

items.title: Symbols that are trading now
items.prose: A market data tool shows how many different symbols have traded recently.
items.question: Write the class `ActiveSymbols(window)`. `tick(symbol, t)` records a trade in `symbol` at time `t`. `active(t)` returns how many distinct symbols traded at a time $s$ with $t - \text{window} < s \le t$. Times never go back across calls. Each call should take constant time on average.

tests.setup:
a = ActiveSymbols(2000)
total = 0
for i in range(100000):
    a.tick((i * 7919) % 30011, i // 3)
    total += a.active(i // 3)

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. They cover the window edge, a repeated symbol, a returning symbol, an idle tool and trades at one time. One test makes 100,000 calls, and a scan of the whole log fails its 5 s limit.

feedback.correct: Keep a queue of recent trades and a count per symbol, and expire old trades on each call.
feedback.generic: A scan of the whole history on each call is too slow for 100,000 calls.

explain.text: Keep a queue of (time, symbol) and a count of queued trades per symbol. Each call first drops trades at or before $t - \text{window}$, lowering counts and removing symbols that reach zero. The answer is the number of symbols counted, and each trade enters and leaves the queue once.

items.question: Write `costliest_desk(df, min_rows)`. It returns the name of the desk with the largest impact slope. Skip a desk with fewer than `min_rows` rows or only one distinct size. Return `None` if no desk qualifies.

feedback.correct: Group by desk, guard the small and flat groups, then pick the largest slope.
feedback.generic: Run it on `FILLS` with `min_rows` 4 and then 3, and compare the two names.

items.title: A slope kept up to date
items.prose: A desk fits slippage $y$ (basis points) on order size $x$ (thousands of shares). Its window holds the last four orders: $(1, 3)$, $(2, 4)$, $(3, 7)$ and $(4, 8)$. It keeps the sums $n$, $\sum x$, $\sum y$, $\sum x^2$ and $\sum xy$, and the slope is $\dfrac{n\sum xy - \sum x \sum y}{n\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2}$.
items.question: Three follow-ups on the same window.

parts.question: A fifth order, $(5, 12)$, arrives. What is the slope over all five?

feedback.correct: The sums become $n = 5$, 15, 34, 55 and 124, so the slope is $(620 - 510)/(275 - 225) = 2.2$.
feedback.generic: Add the new row to every sum, including $n$, before using the formula.

byKey.forgot-n: You kept $n = 4$ after adding the row. The count grows with the sums.
byKey.old-slope: You gave the slope of the first four rows. Add $(5, 12)$ to every sum first.

parts.question: Now the oldest order, $(1, 3)$, leaves the window. What is the slope of the last four?

feedback.correct: Subtract the row from every sum: $n = 4$, 14, 31, 54 and 121. The slope is $(484 - 434)/(216 - 196) = 2.5$.
feedback.generic: Take the leaving row out of every sum, including $n$.

byKey.added-again: You added the leaving row a second time. A departure subtracts from every sum.
byKey.not-removed: You kept the row in. That gives the five-row slope.

parts.question: After a million updates the sums of squares are huge and nearly cancel in the denominator. What is the sound fix?

options.text: Keep sums of deviations from a running mean, so nothing large is subtracted.
Nothing: each removal exactly undoes its addition, so errors cancel.
options.why: Each addition and removal rounds on its own, so the errors build up instead of cancelling.

options.text: Refit from scratch on every update, since running sums cannot be trusted.
options.why: A refit costs a pass over the window each time. Centred sums keep the update at a few operations.

options.text: Use a longer integer for the sums, because the totals overflow.
options.why: The loss is rounding in the subtraction of two nearly equal floats, not overflow.

feedback.correct: Centre the data. Sums of deviations avoid subtracting two huge, nearly equal numbers.
feedback.generic: Ask what is subtracted in the denominator, and how large it is.

explain.text: Adding a row adds to every sum and a departure subtracts from every sum. The slope formula then costs a few operations, not a pass over the window. With huge sums, centre the data first.

items.title: The 96th percentile of 25 messages
items.prose:
A handler timed 25 messages, in µs.

```text
212 198 205 219 201
207 3100 214 203 209
196 211 206 202 2650
208 200 215 204 210
197 213 199 216 205
```

Use the nearest-rank rule. The $p$th percentile is the value at rank $\lceil pn/100 \rceil$ in the sorted list, counting from 1.
items.question: What is the 96th percentile, in µs?

feedback.correct: Rank $\lceil 0.96 \times 25 \rceil = 24$, and the 24th sorted value is 2650 µs.
feedback.generic: Sort the list, find the rank, then read that value.

byKey.mean: You gave the mean, 420 µs. It is twice every typical message and far below both slow ones.
byKey.maximum: You took the largest value. The rank is 24 of 25, so one value sits above it.
byKey.median: You gave the median. The 96th percentile sits near the top of the sorted list.
byKey.interpolated: You interpolated between two values. The nearest-rank rule returns a value from the list.

explain.text: Sorted, the 24th of 25 values is 2650, because $\lceil 0.96 \times 25 \rceil = 24$. The mean is 420 µs, a figure no typical message resembles. Two slow messages lift the mean from about 207 to 420, while the median stays at 207.

items.title: The newest values in a ring
items.prose: A price feed keeps its newest values in a ring of `capacity` slots, a power of two. One counter grows with every push and never wraps back. The value pushed with counter $c$ lives in slot `c & (capacity - 1)`, and a full ring overwrites its oldest value. The code runs on one thread.
items.question: Write `latest_values(xs, capacity, k)`. Push every value of `xs` in order, then return the newest `k` values still held, newest first. If fewer than `k` are held, return them all.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. They cover a ring that wraps, fewer values than `k` and a capacity of 1. Two tests use a `k` above the capacity. They also run 300 pushes through 32 slots and an empty list. A wrong mask or a missing capacity cap fails them.

feedback.correct: Write each value at `count & mask`, then read back from `count - 1` downwards with the same mask.
feedback.generic: Run it by hand with capacity 4 and six values, and write down which slot each value takes.

explain.text: With a power-of-two capacity, `c & (capacity - 1)` keeps the low bits of the counter, which is the counter modulo the capacity. Writing there overwrites the oldest value once the ring is full. Reading from `count - 1` downwards with the same mask returns the newest values first.
